Article Title: Google CEO Sundar Pichai announces EmbeddingGemma 2 model; says it is company’s first open, natively multimodal embedding model
Article Text:
Announcing the new model, Google CEO

Sundar Pichai

said: “Introducing EmbeddingGemma 2, a new open multimodal model that sets the standard for on-device efficiency.

- our first open, natively multimodal embedding model

- handles text, code, image, video, and audio tasks within a lightweight, modular 740M parameter form factor

- ideal for offline, privacy-first RAG when paired with Gemma 4

- outperforms some specialist models more than twice its size

Weights available now on Hugging Face.”

EmbeddingGemma 2: Key capabilities

Native multimodal retrieval: Unlocks search across text, code, images, video, and audio directly in a shared 768-dimensional vector space.

Superior code understanding: Significantly outperforms EmbeddingGemma 1 on code search and technical retrieval, making it ideal for local codebase indexing and agentic code search.

Modular memory footprint: Selectively load only the encoders you need at runtime: 270M (text/code), 440M (text + vision), 570M (text + audio), or 740M (full multimodal), all projecting into the same compatible vector space.

Flexible vector storage: Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) enables dynamic truncation from 768 dimensions down to 128 dimensions, cutting vector database storage requirements while retaining much of the original quality. For instance, at 256 dimensions, most of the full quality of the original embedding on text and code is retained and about 95% on image, video, and speech retrieval

How it works

Text and code (270M base): An adapted Gemma 4 decoder with an 8,192-token context window.

Vision (+170M): A vision encoder that processes images, visual documents (PDFs, slides, charts), and video frames.

Audio (+300M): A dedicated speech and sound encoder that directly ingests raw audio.

Modular loading: You only load what you need. Run text-only at 270M parameters, add vision for 440M parameters, or load the full multimodal model at 740M parameters.

Shared tokenizer & audio encoder with Gemma 4: When paired with Gemma 4 in an on-device RAG pipeline, both models share the same text tokenizer and audio encoder architecture, reducing the total memory footprint.

Google has launched EmbeddingGemma 2, an open multimodal embedding model for devices. The launch comes a year after the company introduced EmbeddingGemma for developers last year. For those unaware, an embedding model is a machine learning tool that turns complex data like words, sentences, images, or audio into a list of numbers called a vector. Built on the Gemma 4 architecture and released under a commercially permissive Apache 2.0 license, EmbeddingGemma 2 has 740 million parameters, making it optimal for on-device inference. It can help find a specific video clip from a voice memo, or search through hours of audio recordings based on a text query, all processed by a single, natively multimodal model.EmbeddingGemma 2 is designed to provide a single, compact open model released under the Apache 2.0 license, delivering exceptional multimodal performance for its size. Based on Gemma 4, this sub-1B model maps text, code, images, video, and audio into a unified 768-dimensional space. Its modular architecture can scale from 270M parameters for text and code up to 740M parameters for all modalities. Key capabilities of the EmbeddingGemma include:Google says that all inputs are processed through the shared backbone and their resulting embeddings occupy the same dimensional space:
Article Summary: Google has launched EmbeddingGemma 2, an open multimodal embedding model for devices. Based on Gemma 4, this sub-1B model maps text, code, images, video, and audio into a unified 768-dimensional space. Its modular architecture can scale from 270M parameters for text and code up to 740M for all modalities.

Article Title: Scientists build ‘mind-reading’ AI program that can tell what you are thinking and recreates photos with striking accuracy
Article Text:
Major leap from grainy predecessors

How scientists solved data problem with a dual-translation ‘encoder’

Irani explained how the algorithmic framework generated its own training data:

A group of Israeli scientists have engineered an advanced artificial intelligence (AI) system called Brain-IT that can interpret what a person is picturing in his mind and then using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data, reconstruct those mental photos with remarkable precision. Detailed in a research submission to the International Conference on Learning Representations, the system yields visual outputs that closely reflect the real images viewed by subjects across both structural layouts and semantic meanings.The visual recreations demonstrated by the team range from basic street stop signs to intricate scenes like a tomato-and-olive pizza that captures the exact slice count envisioned by the viewer, essentially acting virtually like a digital replica of internal cognitive thought.While AI brain-decoding projects have surfaced before, Brain-IT establishes a dramatically higher benchmark for speed and fidelity. In 2017 (Purdue University), early models developed in Indiana could infer the general category of an image a participant imagined but the visual recreations were noticeably blurry and indistinct.In 2022 (Japan), researchers applied diffusion-style architectures to generate sharper approximations, though the framework depended heavily on intermediate text-to-image translation.Brain-IT has been developed under the direction of Michal Irani at the Weizmann Institute of Science, and mirrors target images with minute accuracy while completing the analysis process within just one hour, cutting down significantly from multi-hour processing runs required by previous systems.A major challenge in neuroimaging research is the physical and financial limitation of gathering human data. To train the architecture, researchers gathered records of eight subjects observing more than 70,000 pictures inside fMRI machines. As eight individuals represent a modest cohort for training frontier AI, the team bypassed the need for round-the-clock machine sessions by creating an “encoder” shortcut that enabled bidirectional translation.“We realized that by translating back and forth – from a random image that had never been viewed in an fMRI machine, to a predicted brain scan, and then back to the image we started with – the models would effectively build themselves a massive dataset. In this way, during training, the models would learn to generate scans that encode images effectively, even though those fMRI scans had never actually been performed.”Through this dual-decoding workflow, the system pinpointed 128 functional brain regions, including uncovering a mixture of familiar zones alongside newly identified areas, that carry out comparable visual processing tasks across different people. Certain clusters responded predictably to culinary imagery, others ignited when subjects viewed athletics and distinct neural pathways corresponded to indoor versus outdoor settings.The researchers see practical applications for the breakthrough, especially as an assistive communication system for paralysed patients who have lost physical speech or movement.
Article Summary: Brain-IT has been developed under the direction of Michal Irani at the Weizmann Institute of Science. It mirrors target images with minute accuracy while completing the analysis process within just one hour, cutting down significantly from multi-hour processing runs required by previous systems.

Article Title: AI Data Security : Everyone wants an AI agent but almost nobody is asking where the data goes
Article Text:
Start with some very simple questions

“Trust us” isn’t enough

AI needs to earn our trust

By: Krish Ramineni, Co-founder & CEO, Fireflies.ai

Everyone wants an AI agent right now. We want AI that can prepare us for meetings, answer emails, search through our work, update the CRM and eventually just get things done for us. That’s where this is going. AI is moving from something you open when you need help to something that is always there, working alongside you. Less like another tool and more like an AI teammate.But there’s one question we’re not asking enough: Where does all that data go?Because the more useful your AI teammate becomes, the more it needs to know about you and your company. If it’s preparing you for a meeting, it might need access to your calendar, past meetings and documents. If it’s writing an email, it might need access to your inbox. If it’s updating your CRM, it needs access to customer information. And if you eventually want it doing work for you all day, it may need access to almost everything you use at work. The most useful AI teammate may also be the one that knows the most about your work. That’s why security matters so much.Before a company gives an AI access to its information, it should know what happens to that information. Is our data being used to train AI models? Where is it stored? How long is it kept? Who can see it? Can we delete it? Can we control what the AI has access to? Can we see what actions it has taken? And what happens when another AI company or model is involved?These sound like basic questions. But as we give AI access to more of our work, they become incredibly important.Security shouldn’t be something companies think about after they buy an AI product. It should be part of deciding which AI products they trust in the first place.Microsoft says Copilot follows a company’s existing permissions and that its business data isn’t used to train its foundation models. Google says Gemini for Workspace follows existing Workspace protections and doesn’t use customer data to train its generative AI models without permission. Zoom says it doesn’t use customer communications to train its own or third-party AI models. There’s a reason companies are starting to make these promises much clearer. Security is becoming part of the product.This becomes even more important when AI has access to conversations. Think about what gets discussed in meetings: customers, employees, hiring, strategy, financials and plans that may never be written down anywhere else. Companies should know exactly what happens to that information. At Fireflies, for example, we don’t use customer meeting content to train AI models. We require third-party vendors handling meeting content to follow zero-data-retention requirements. We also maintain SOC 2 Type II, GDPR and HIPAA compliance. “Trust us” isn’t a security policy. Companies should be able to understand where their data goes, who can access it and what controls they have over it.Banning AI isn’t the answer. Some companies may look at these risks and decide the safest thing to do is block AI altogether. I don’t think that solves the problem. People are already using AI to write, research, prepare for meetings and get work done faster. If their company blocks these tools, some employees will simply use personal accounts or other apps the company doesn’t know about. Now the company has even less control over where its data is going.A better approach is to give employees AI products the company has actually reviewed and approved and then set clear rules around what those products can see and what they’re allowed to do.This gets even more important as AI starts taking action. There’s a big difference between drafting an email and sending it. There’s a difference between suggesting a CRM update and making the change. There’s a difference between finding a document and sharing it with someone.The more AI can do on your behalf, the more control you need over what it’s allowed to do.For the last few years, everyone has been focused on making AI smarter. Can it answer better questions? Can it understand more? Can it do more work?Those things still matter. But as AI becomes more deeply connected to our work, there’s another question that matters just as much: Can we trust it?Today, a company might use AI to take meeting notes. Tomorrow, that same AI teammate could prepare you for meetings, search your email and Slack, update your CRM, follow up with customers and take care of work across dozens of apps.Every time we give it another ability, we’re also giving it more access. And that means companies need to know that their AI teammate is looking at the right information, for the right reason, and doing only what it has permission to do.The goal isn’t just to build AI that knows more. It’s to build AI that we can trust to do more.
Article Summary: AI is moving from something you open when you need help to something that is always there. “Trust us” isn’t a security policy. Companies should be able to understand where their data goes, who can access it and what controls they have over it.

Article Title: Claude Code creator Boris Cherny shares what not to miss while giving prompt to Claude; says: There's no secret to ...
Article Text:
Anthropic’s Boris Cherny reveals what matters on prompting AI today

The prompt that caught attention

Anthropic’s Claude Code creator, Boris Cherny has offered a simple piece of advice to users who are trying to get better results from AI models. In a post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) Cherny asked the users to talk to Claude the same way they would talk to a coworker. As per Cherny users no longer need highly structured and very detailed prompts for most tasks, as modern AI models are increasingly capable of figuring out how to achieve a goal on their own. In the post shared on X, Cherny revealed that he was surprised that people were surprised by the way he prompts Claude. “Talk to Claude the way you would a coworker. There's no secret to prompting. There's no need to be overly scaffolded or prescriptive for most tasks. Give Claude a goal, and it will figure it out,” he wrote.Cherny contrasted the current approach with the early days of Claude's Sonnet 3.5 models, when the exact wording of a prompt mattered a great deal. Today's models, he suggested, need less hand-holding on the "how" and more clarity about the "what."He said it is now much more important to communicate three things to the model:1. What you want it to do2. How much effort you want it to spend3. How it should verify that it did the right thingThe comments align with advice Cherny has shared in public discussions, where he has argued that many users make the mistake of over-specifying every step instead of clearly defining the desired outcome.Modern AI models are often better used by describing the goal and success criteria rather than dictating a rigid sequence of actions.Alongside his comments, Cherny shared an example of a prompt he uses with Claude.In the example, he asked the AI to create an interactive artefact about a recent podcast episode on Home Depot's acquisition strategy. Rather than providing detailed step-by-step instructions, he described the end goal: a visually rich, interactive experience that highlights key business lessons.The prompt asked Claude to make the output “beautiful and interactive,” focus on business wisdom from the episode, use extensive reasoning and iteration, and incorporate elements such as watercolour illustrations, historical photographs and visual storytelling inspired by publications such as The New Yorker and The New York Times.Notably, the prompt emphasised the desired outcome and quality bar rather than prescribing a detailed process, reflecting the prompting philosophy Cherny advocates.
Article Summary: Anthropic’s Claude Code creator, Boris Cherny has offered a simple piece of advice to users who are trying to get better results from AI models. In a post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) Cherny asked the users to talk to Claude the same way they would talk to a coworker.

Article Title: Cab driver allegedly snatches farmer’s phone, transfers Rs 90,000
Article Text: Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar: A cab driver allegedly snatched a 66-year-old farmer’s mobile phone and used a digital payment platform to siphon off Rs 90,000 from his bank account in three transactions, police said.Jawahar Nagar police registered an FIR against cab driver Deepak Simon Shelke and Kunal Deepak Shelke following a complaint by Dwarkadas Harinarayan Baheti, a resident of Kasliwal Marble in the Beed Bypass area.According to the complaint, the incident occurred near the Devi temple in Vishnunagar between 3.38pm on Oct 1 and 10am on Oct 2. Baheti alleged that Deepak forcibly snatched his Samsung Galaxy A15 phone.The accused allegedly accessed PhonePe on the phone and transferred Rs 90,000 in three transactions to a bank account held in Kunal’s name.Baheti told police that he could not lodge the complaint immediately as his wife was unwell. He approached police after her condition improved.Jawahar Nagar police are investigating the alleged roles of both the cab driver and the recipient of the money. Sub-inspector Kamble is conducting the probe.
Article Summary: Jawahar Nagar police registered an FIR against cab driver Deepak Simon Shelke and Kunal Deepak Shelke following a complaint. Dwarkadas Harinarayan Baheti, a resident of Kasliwal Marble in the Beed Bypass area, alleged that Deepak forcibly snatched his Samsung Galaxy A15.

Article Title: Round the clock ration to be available in Nashik with new grain ATM
Article Text:
Grain ATM to be launched by supply department in Nashik

Nashik

:





For ration card holders, collecting the monthly quota of wheat and rice often means planning the day around a visit to the ration shop. They have to arrive when the shop is open, wait in a queue and hope the e-PoS machine works. There are also complaints of receiving less grain than their entitlement.That routine could soon change in Nashik. In a first-of-its-kind initiative in Maharashtra , an automatic grain dispensing machine is expected to start functioning at Nashik Road by mid-Oct. Think of it as an ATM for foodgrain. Authenticate yourself, place your bag and collect your quota.More importantly, beneficiaries can do it at a time that suits them. The machine will operate 24x7, freeing families from ration shop timings and long waits. It is also expected to cut human intervention in weighing and dispensing grain, addressing complaints of short-weighing.The food and civil supplies department is setting up the facility on a pilot basis at the old govt foodgrain warehouse at Nashik Road. Nagpur is also among the state’s pioneer centres selected for the experiment.“The initiative aims to address recurring operational issues faced by beneficiaries under the PDS, including frequent technical glitches in e-PoS machines, erratic shop hours, long waiting times and complaints regarding short-weighing,” officiating district supply officer Ramesh Gaikwad said.The machine can store 100 quintals of grain, with 50 quintals each of wheat and rice.For beneficiaries, the process is designed to be simple.They will enter their Aadhaar or ration card number and authenticate their identity through a fingerprint scan. Their entitlement will appear on the screen. Once verified, the machine will automatically measure and release the grain into their bag.It can dispense up to 50kg within five minutes, officials said.The facility will cater to beneficiaries under the Antyodaya Anna Yojana and Priority Household schemes. Migrant workers covered by the One Nation One Ration Card system can also use it, removing geographical restrictions on where they collect their grain.That could make the system particularly useful for workers whose schedules often clash with ration shop hours.Solar power backup is another feature intended to keep the machine running during electricity outages. Local ration dealers will oversee the facility and refill wheat and rice when stocks run low.The experiment does not, however, eliminate ration shops altogether. The automated unit is meant specifically for free grain and does not have a payment facility. If govt announces items that have to be purchased, including supplies distributed under special schemes, those will continue to require a fair price shop dealer to collect payment and hand over the goods.
Article Summary: Machine will operate 24x7, freeing families from ration shop timings and long waits. It is also expected to cut human intervention in weighing and dispensing grain, addressing complaints of short-weighing. Facility will cater to beneficiaries under Antyodaya Anna Yojana and Priority Household schemes.

Article Title: Florida man arrested after placing virus on woman’s computer, sharing private info in more than 100 TikTok videos
Article Text:
Florida man published more than 100 videos on Tik Tok

Woman alleged a virus was placed on her computer

Investigators also examined alleged location tracking

Police seized electronic devices

Earlier stalking allegations were dropped

Prosecutors revived the computer case

A 36-year-old Florida man was arrested after investigators accused him of gaining unauthorised access to a woman’s computer and posting private information involving women in more than 100 TikTok videos. Mark Stephen Asea of Port St. Lucie was booked into the St Lucie County Jail on September 30 on a felony computer-access charge, with his bond set at $35,000. The case followed an investigation into allegations involving at least two women, including claims that Asea had remotely accessed a computer, obtained passwords and private material, and discussed personal information in his online videos. Investigators also examined claims involving location data, purchases and private conversations. Asea’s earlier stalking allegations were dropped, but prosecutors later revived the computer-related case in September.The investigation centred partly on Asea’s TikTok account, where police say he published more than 100 videos involving one of the women. According to the police affidavit cited by local and national media, some of the videos allegedly contained details about the woman’s personal life and information that investigators believed he should not have had access to.Detectives reviewed videos in which Asea discussed information including a password, phone or device details, purchases and location-related information. The woman told investigators that some of the information had been shared privately and questioned how Asea had obtained it.Asea has presented himself online using descriptions including “grey hat hacker” and “demonologist”. His online profiles have also used terms such as “cybersecurity engineer”, according to reporting based on the police investigation.A separate allegation involved another woman who told investigators that Asea had previously helped her remotely with a computer problem. According to the affidavit, the woman had allowed Asea to access her computer remotely in October 2025 while he helped troubleshoot an application. She later became concerned after allegedly learning that he had installed a programme or virus that could allow continued access without her knowledge or permission.The woman also told police that a photograph from a private conversation later appeared in one of Asea’s TikTok videos. Investigators examined the circumstances surrounding the image and the alleged access to her electronic device. The computer-related allegation ultimately became the focus of the criminal charge filed against Asea in September.Police also investigated allegations that Asea had access to information about a woman’s location. According to the affidavit, detectives reviewed online material in which Asea allegedly discussed GPS information connected to the woman’s phone. The investigation examined whether he had obtained information that would allow him to determine where she was.The case also involved allegations concerning private communications and personal information. Investigators were particularly interested in how information that appeared in Asea’s online content had been obtained and whether it came from devices or accounts that he was not authorised to access.The allegations formed part of a wider investigation into Asea’s interactions with the women and his use of information in his social-media content.The investigation eventually led authorities to search Asea’s residence and collect electronic equipment for examination. According to court documents described in media reports, investigators seized items including computers, mobile phones, external hard drives, USB storage devices, an iPad, a Dell laptop and other networking equipment.Authorities sought to examine the devices for evidence that could establish how information had been obtained or stored. Investigators were interested in material such as passwords, messages, account information, financial records, browser history and location data. The forensic examination was significant because the allegations involved information that investigators believed may have originated from electronic devices or private accounts.Asea's current case follows an earlier criminal investigation. He was initially arrested in April 2026 in connection with allegations that included stalking and unauthorised computer access. However, prosecutors filed a “No Information” in May, meaning the charges then under consideration were not pursued at that stage.A separate civil proceeding also involved a woman seeking protection through a stalking injunction. A temporary order was issued in July, but the case was later dismissed and the injunction was dissolved in September. The criminal investigation nevertheless returned to court later in the year.On September 24, prosecutors reopened the criminal case and filed a new information against Asea. The revived prosecution focuses on a felony allegation involving unauthorised access to a computer or electronic device. Asea was subsequently booked into the St Lucie County Jail on September 30. His bond was set at $35,000.The current case is narrower than the allegations that surrounded the earlier investigation. The stalking allegations that were previously dropped were not simply reinstated as part of the September filing. Instead, the active criminal charge concerns the alleged unauthorised computer access. Asea is due to appear for arraignment on November 19, according to reports citing court records.
Article Summary: Mark Stephen Asea of Port St. Lucie was booked into the St Lucie County Jail on September 30 on a felony computer-access charge. The case followed an investigation into allegations involving at least two women, including claims that Asea had remotely accessed a computer, obtained passwords and private material. Investigators also examined claims involving location data, purchases and private conversations.

Article Title: In 2019, Oregon rebuilt 7.5 miles of Juntura Cutoff Road with recycled pavement and foamed asphalt, saving more than $2.5 million
Article Text:
Representation of a rural road being rebuilt using foamed asphalt, with construction machinery preparing and compacting the recycled roadway base. Image Credits: ChatGPT.

Recycling the road in place

Keeping traffic moving

Cold in-place recycling using foamed asphalt. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

A different way to rebuild roads

In 2019, Oregon tried a different approach to rebuilding a badly damaged rural road. Instead of removing the old pavement and starting again with new materials, the existing road was recycled in place using foamed asphalt. The method saved more than $2.5 million compared with conventional reconstruction, while also reducing the construction period by almost a month.According to the RoadResource , the project involved a 7.5-mile section of Juntura Cutoff Road, which connected the EP Minerals diatomite mine with US Highway 20. Years of heavy truck traffic had left the road with deep cracks, potholes and sections where the asphalt had completely failed. With the road serving as an important route for mine traffic, keeping it available during construction was also a major consideration.In the case study, the original reconstruction estimate was about $6.7 million. The alternative used cold in-place recycling with foamed asphalt, a process that allowed the existing pavement material to be reused rather than removed and hauled away. The project ultimately saved more than $2.5 million, or about 37% compared with conventional reconstruction, while recycling 100% of the existing material in place.The process involved milling about eight inches of the existing asphalt along with part of the underlying road base. The reclaimed material was then mixed with foamed asphalt, cement and water before being compacted and shaped into a new base. The Oregon Department of Transportation referred to the approach as CIREAM, a form of cold in-place recycling that uses foamed asphalt. Foamed asphalt is made by adding a small amount of water to hot asphalt binder, causing it to expand temporarily. The expanded binder can then spread through the reclaimed pavement material and bind it together. This allows the old road material to be reused in the new base without processing the entire mixture as conventional hot-mix asphalt.The recycling method was especially practical because Juntura Cutoff Road was the mine’s main access route, making a long closure difficult. Instead of removing the old pavement and road base and bringing in completely new material, much of the existing road was reused to form the new base. This meant less material had to be hauled away and replaced, while mine traffic could continue using the route during the work.The recycled base also became useful when the construction schedule changed. Crews had initially expected to place the 2.5-inch layer of PG 64-28 hot-mix asphalt within seven days, but the paving was delayed by about a month. In the meantime, the recycled base was left in place and kept hydrated until the final surface could be laid. The delay therefore did not mean that the newly reconstructed base had to be removed or redone. It remained part of the road while the project waited for the final paving stage.The approach was consistent with findings from wider research on foamed-asphalt cold-recycled mixtures. A study published in Construction and Building Materials found that these mixtures could provide useful engineering properties, including good water stability and high modulus, when the materials and pavement layers were properly designed. The findings help explain why foamed-asphalt recycling could work as more than simply a way to reuse old pavement: it could also provide a functional structural layer within a new road.The Juntura Cutoff Project showed that the old road could be reused as a construction material asset. The project avoided removing large amounts of old pavement and hauling in new aggregate, instead reusing material already on site. RoadResource also notes that it is possible to use the road for 20 years if maintenance activities are carried out. The road was found to have a performance comparable to that of a traditional road reconstruction project. These estimations are solely associated with the project and do not provide evidence for the longevity of all foamed roads.For the State of Oregon, the most immediate outcome was that of cost and time savings. The state now had a way to repair a badly damaged road using the existing surface material while keeping the road open and saving more than $2.5 million. This project showed that in-place recycling can help reduce road rehabilitation costs and time.
Article Summary: Oregon tried a different approach to rebuilding a badly damaged rural road. Instead of removing the old pavement and starting again with new materials, the existing road was recycled in place. The method saved more than $2.5 million compared with conventional reconstruction, while also reducing the construction period by almost a month.

Article Title: In 2024, researchers turned discarded plastic bottles and stone into pothole-repair surfacing; strength, stiffness and durability exceeded typical road-infrastructure requirements
Article Text:
Representative image of workers repairing a pothole with road surfacing made from recycled plastic bottles and stone. Image Credits: ChatGPT.

Turning plastic waste into a road-repair material

The best-performing mixture

A groundbreaking study from the University of Dodoma in Tanzania introduces an innovative pothole repair technique that combines melted PET plastic bottles with sand and gravel. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

From laboratory success to real-world roads

Potholes are a familiar problem for road users, damaging vehicles, slowing traffic and creating hazards for cyclists and pedestrians. Repairing them usually involves asphalt-based mixtures, but these materials can be expensive, and poorly executed patches may deteriorate under repeated traffic loads and exposure to water. Researchers have been exploring whether discarded plastic can offer an alternative, tackling road maintenance and plastic waste at the same time.In December 2024, a study published in Frontiers in Engineering and Built Environment investigated a different approach: melting waste plastic bottles and combining the material with sand and crushed stone to produce a surface for pothole repairs. The research, conducted at the University of Dodoma in Tanzania, found that the best-performing mixture exceeded conventional benchmarks in several mechanical tests.The research addressed two related problems: plastic pollution and road-maintenance costs. PET (polyethene terephthalate) is widely used in beverage packaging and discarded after use. Finding a use for this type of plastic could help divert some of it from disposal while reducing dependence on conventional construction materials. To experiment, the scientists collected used PET bottles from the University of Dodoma campus.The bottles were washed, cut into pieces measuring 10–20 mm, and dried in the sun for 24 hours. The plastic was then heated to 280°C before being mixed with sand and gravel in different proportions. The optimum mixture was later identified as 30% PET, 30% sand and 40% gravel by weight.Mixes were formed with varying percentages of PET, sand, and gravel to find out which one gave better mechanical results. This included mixes made entirely of PET as well as mixes with varying amounts of plastic and aggregate. The scientists created samples out of these materials and analysed them in laboratories. This was done with the intention of coming up with a formulation that can give the stability and stiffness required for pothole repair.The best-performing mixture contained 30% PET plastic, 30% sand and 40% gravel by weight. It was observed that the equilibrium ratio between the plastic binding agent and mineral aggregate components is crucial; an excess of plastic would make the mixture less strong. The right balance of sand and gravel made the mixture stronger and denser. Three factors were considered in analysing the material's behaviour.First was the Marshall Stability, which reflects resistance to deformation. The optimum mixture scored 59.78 kilonewtons (kN), compared with the usual 7–15 kN for common asphalt mixtures. The second test was the indirect tensile strength test, which evaluates a material’s resistance to tensile stress and cracking. This formulation had a tensile strength of 5,909 kilopascals (kPa). Third, the stiffness modulus was used to evaluate how the material responds to applied forces. In this test, they obtained a result of 36,145 megapascals (MPa). Based on these findings, the material met the mechanical requirements set by the researchers.These results suggest a way to use waste bottles as a building material while reducing reliance on traditional road-repair materials. Using locally available sand and gravel may also help in areas with tight road-maintenance budgets and abundant plastic waste. There are some issues that have not yet been clarified. Field tests need to be performed to determine the behaviour of the composite in a real-world setting in the presence of traffic, changing temperatures, and moisture.The energy required for melting should also be considered. Heating PET to 280 degrees Celsius takes energy and requires proper safety controls. Any assessment of the approach's environmental benefits would need to consider processing energy, possible emissions, worker safety, and how the material changes over time. Cost should also be considered. Even though the bottles are not costly, gathering, cleaning, cutting, and melting them does take some effort. A comparison with traditional patching should include these costs, along with installation and maintenance.For now, the study is seen as a promising laboratory result rather than a direct substitute for asphalt. Its primary value is to show that used plastic bottles may act as a binding agent in a sand-and-gravel repair mix without bitumen or cement. If further field tests confirm its strength and reliability, it could become another tool for pothole repair and a useful application for waste plastic bottles. It remains to be seen whether the product will work as reliably in the field as it does in the lab.
Article Summary: Researchers from the University of Dodoma in Tanzania have created a pothole repair technique that combines melted PET plastic bottles with sand and gravel. The best-performing mixture exceeded conventional benchmarks in several mechanical tests. The research addressed two related problems: plastic pollution and road-maintenance costs.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.
Article Summary: A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.

Article Title: How to get your CIBIL credit score without a PAN card
Article Text:
Your credit score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity.

What is a CIBIL score?

How to get your CIBIL Credit score without a PAN Card

Factors affecting your CIBIL score

CIBIL credit score : Understanding your creditworthiness is pivotal in today's financial landscape, especially when seeking loans or credit cards. The Credit Information Bureau (India) Limited, commonly known as CIBIL, plays an important role in this regard by providing credit scores to borrowers.According to ET, credit score helps banks make informed decisions about extending credit cards and loans. Your credit history influences your CIBIL score , which is calculated using a special method.Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.1. Go to the official CIBIL website and click on 'Personal CIBIL score,' then 'Get Your Free CIBIL score.' Follow the link provided and fill in all the required details.2. If you don’t have a PAN Card, you can use an alternative identification such as Passport, Voter ID, Driver’s License, or Ration Card. Enter the number of the chosen ID.3. Provide your date of birth, PIN code, and select your state. Finally, enter your mobile number and click on ‘Accept and Continue’.4. Authenticate your identity by entering the OTP (One-Time Password) delivered to your mobile device on the next screen. Click 'Continue' to proceed.5. Choose whether you want to link the device with your account. Select 'Yes' or 'No' based on your preference.6. Upon successful registration, you will see a page confirming that 'You have successfully registered!'7. Click on ‘Go to Dashboard’ to access and view your CIBIL score.The factors influencing the new CIBIL score, as stated on the CIBIL website, include:1. Depth of credit: This refers to the duration of your existing credit history, calculated from the opening date of your oldest credit account.2. Long-term trend of outstanding balances: The overall trend of outstanding balances over time affects your score.3. Transaction history on credit cards: How you manage transactions on your credit cards impacts your score.4. Ratio of actual repayment amount to total amount due: This ratio indicates your repayment behavior and influences your score accordingly.5. Number of new accounts opened and number of accounts closed: Opening or closing accounts can affect your score, so managing these actions wisely is important.

Article Title: Florida scientists used machine learning to predict when giant Burmese pythons are most likely to be caught; weather and moon phases matter
Article Text:
Representative AI image

Machine learning targets high-impact Burmese pythons

Large reproductive females can have an outsized impact

Weather and moon phases shape survey conditions

South Florida data provide a real-world test

A new way to measure the success of python removal

Florida scientists have used machine learning to identify when python-removal surveys are most likely to capture Burmese pythons with the greatest potential to influence population growth. Researchers from the University of Florida combined demographic information about individual snakes with environmental and survey conditions to develop a Weighted Removal Index, which assigns greater importance to pythons with higher reproductive and survival potential. The study found that survey value was associated with factors including temperature, humidity, season and lunar phase. Large reproductive females emerged as particularly important targets, while warmer, more humid conditions and waning lunar phases were associated with higher-value captures. The findings could help wildlife managers direct limited personnel and resources towards removal periods that are more likely to have a meaningful effect on the invasive population. This smarter, data-driven approach to invasive species management shows real promise, potentially helping conservationists maximize their limited resources by focusing python-removal efforts precisely when captures matter most for population control.Published in Ecological Applications, the study addresses a problem that conventional python-removal programmes can overlook: the number of snakes captured does not necessarily reflect the ecological value of those removals. A juvenile and a mature reproductive female may count equally as individual captures, but their potential contributions to the future population are very different.To account for that difference, the researchers developed the Weighted Removal Index (WRI). The index incorporates demographic characteristics that influence a snake's expected contribution to population growth. It gives greater weight to individuals with characteristics associated with higher survival and reproductive potential.The approach allows researchers to evaluate an entire survey according to the demographic value of the snakes captured rather than simply counting animals. This distinction is particularly important for Burmese pythons, whose population dynamics are strongly influenced by the survival and reproduction of mature individuals.The researchers then combined the WRI with environmental and operational information to determine which conditions were associated with surveys yielding greater demographic value.The demographic weighting places particular importance on mature, reproductive females. A large female that survives to reproduce can contribute substantially to future population growth, while a smaller juvenile faces a higher risk of dying before reaching reproductive age.This makes the removal of a reproductive female potentially more consequential than the removal of several snakes with lower reproductive potential. The study's framework therefore shifts attention from the simple question of how many pythons are caught to which individuals are removed from the population.The researchers compared three modelling approaches to determine whether these high-value surveys could be predicted: generalised additive models, boosted regression trees and neural networks. The neural network produced the strongest performance when evaluated against held-out data.It achieved a balanced accuracy of 0.703 in predicting survey success and recorded the lowest prediction error for survey WRI, with a root mean squared error of 5.50. The result indicates that environmental and survey information contained useful signals for anticipating when removal efforts were likely to produce greater demographic value.Environmental conditions emerged as important predictors of survey WRI. The researchers found higher values under warmer and more humid conditions, with the pattern also varying according to season.WRI was elevated on warmer days early in the wet season and on cooler days during the dry season. Such patterns are consistent with the biology of Burmese pythons, which are ectothermic and depend on environmental conditions to regulate their body temperature and activity.Lunar conditions also contributed to the model. Surveys conducted during waning lunar phases were associated with higher survey WRI, adding another environmental variable that managers could consider when planning removal operations.The significance of these findings lies in their combined use. Rather than treating weather, season or lunar phase as isolated predictors, the modelling framework considers multiple factors simultaneously to identify periods when surveys are more likely to produce captures with greater demographic importance.One particularly notable result involved the winter months. January and February can produce relatively few captures when success is measured simply by the number of snakes removed. However, their WRI could be comparatively high because the snakes captured during these periods included a greater proportion of mature males and females.The research drew on data from the South Florida Water Management District's Python Elimination Program, giving the researchers access to information collected during operational python-removal efforts.The work builds on earlier UF/IFAS research examining thousands of surveys in South Florida. Previous analysis found that python searches were generally more productive during the wet season and identified particular times and environmental conditions associated with increased detection.The new study adds a demographic dimension to those findings. Instead of using survey success solely as a measure of the number of animals detected, researchers assessed the characteristics of the pythons removed and calculated their potential contribution to future population growth.That distinction could be valuable in South Florida, where Burmese pythons have become an established invasive predator. They are difficult to detect because of their cryptic behaviour and ability to remain concealed in vegetation and other habitats. Their broad diet also allows them to prey on numerous native species, making population control a significant conservation challenge.With removal efforts requiring substantial time and manpower, managers have to make decisions about when and where to deploy those resources. A forecasting system that identifies conditions associated with higher-value captures could provide an additional tool for those decisions.The researchers' approach ultimately challenges the idea that the success of an invasive-species removal programme should be judged primarily by its capture total. Two surveys can produce very different numbers of snakes while having substantially different implications for future population growth.The Weighted Removal Index offers a way to quantify that difference. By combining demographic characteristics with machine-learning predictions, managers could potentially identify periods when their efforts are more likely to remove mature or otherwise demographically important pythons.The framework could be particularly useful in areas where Burmese pythons are beginning to establish or expand their range. Removing reproductive individuals early in an invasion may have greater consequences for population growth than removing the same number of lower-value individuals later.
Article Summary: Researchers from the University of Florida combined demographic information about individual snakes with environmental and survey conditions to develop a Weighted Removal Index. The index assigns greater importance to pythons with higher reproductive and survival potential. Large reproductive females emerged as particularly important targets. Warm, more humid conditions and waning lunar phases were associated with higher-value captures.

Article Title: Who will we be when AI agents do the chores we secretly enjoy
Article Text:

What they call friction is the part people enjoy

Choosing is how we find out what we like

An agent can only serve the person you have already been

The hours it saves have nowhere better to go

Agents are most useful where we were never attached

There are chores we complain about and would never give up. Choosing a birthday present for a friend. Putting together a playlist for a long drive. Spending an evening choosing a frame for a print we finally bought, losing twenty minutes to a stranger's bookshelf on Instagram, coming home from a grocery run with a snack nobody put on the list. They eat into our free time, and they are often the best part of it.AI agents are being built to take exactly these jobs away. Where a chatbot answers questions, an agent goes off and does the work, signing in to websites, filling in forms, comparing prices, making the booking and paying for it. This year the technology moved out of developer tools and onto ordinary phones, with a long line of new agents queuing up behind the first wave, and the people building it speak about the errands of daily life as the easy bit. Sam Altman , unveiling OpenAI 's agents last week, described booking a table or a flight as "trivial relative to what the technology can do."Every agent is sold on the time it gives back. I have been letting one run bits of my own life, and the time it saved me came from the jobs I was glad to lose. The ones I would happily have kept were the ones it fumbled.Very few of the people building these tools have asked what we were doing with that time, or who we turn into once the errands we enjoy go the same way as the ones we hate.Silicon Valley's working assumption is that time spent on a task is time wasted. Every agent demo is built on it: travel bookings, concert tickets, online shopping, dinner reservations, a standing watch on property listings so a flat-hunter never has to browse a real estate site again. Each one is presented as a cost to be cut. For a lot of people, though, those tasks are what a quiet night on the sofa looks like, idly browsing flats in a city they will never move to, or comparing ticket prices for a gig they may not even go to.The effort is often where the value sits. Behavioural researchers call it the IKEA effect, after studies published in 2011 in which people valued flat-pack furniture and origami they had put together themselves well above identical pieces made by someone else. Gamers have always understood this, since a game is a set of obstacles we choose for the pleasure of clearing them, and I have never met a player who wanted a bot to beat the final boss for them. A record you dug out of a secondhand crate means more than the same album served up by an algorithm. A plant you nursed back from the brink feels more like yours than one delivered in full bloom. Take the work out and the result still arrives, minus the attachment that made it worth having.The industry keeps missing this because of who it builds for. People who pay for AI are five times as likely to use agents, according to Menlo Ventures and Morning Consult, and the heavy user they sketch is a millennial parent with a postgraduate degree and a job in tech or finance, someone with more money than time. That person really does experience a child's birthday party as a project to be managed. Most people have fewer projects and more Sunday afternoons, and they tend to spend those afternoons doing exactly what the demos want to automate.Josh Miller, founder of The Browser Company, argued in a post that went viral in August that almost nobody outside the industry was using agents and the general public didn't much care. He also noticed that nearly every AI lab he met described its vision by citing Her, a film about a lonely man who hands his inner life to an operating system and ends with the operating system leaving him. It is a revealing blueprint, a version of the good life in which software handles the living.I trained as an engineer before I drifted into journalism, and in engineering, friction is energy lost. In a free evening, a fair amount of it is the reason we bothered, and stripping it out makes the task faster without making anyone's weekend better.Holiday planning is the cleanest example. It begins long before the flight, in a dozen hotel tabs, a group-chat argument over whether the 6am departure is worth the saving, and a long squint at a balcony photo to work out how much of the advertised sea view is car park. A Dutch study that followed more than 1,500 adults in 2010 found holidaymakers were happiest in the weeks before they left, with the lift fading soon after they got back. An agent can compress all of that into a confirmation email, and in doing so it removes the stretch of the trip people enjoy most.The agent I have been using is Instinct, from a start-up that has just raised a billion dollars. There is no app to learn. You text it, message it on WhatsApp or call it, it costs nothing to use, and it works your phone and laptop the way a person would, reading your email, chasing threads you dropped and arranging things on your behalf.In Berlin, I asked it for a few cafés near my hotel, the sort of question a friend who had been there could answer in one text. What came back was a list of cafés that had already closed, a couple that were a good half-hour away, and menus that didn't match what the places were actually serving. Public transport went worse, with directions that created more confusion than they cleared, and I ended up back on Google Maps, working out the routes myself. In hindsight that was the better outcome, because learning a city's trains and stumbling on your own coffee is half the reason to be somewhere new.Shopping is where the gap gets widest. Window shopping, trying on trainers you already know you won't buy, bookmarking some odd kitchen gadget at midnight, even standing in an aisle deciding between two brands of detergent, are all small ways of working out what we like. I compare phones and laptops for a living, and I still spend evenings comparing camera lenses I have no plan to buy, which is how I learnt which focal lengths I care about and which compromises I can live with.There is a version of agent shopping I would happily sign up for. If I have already found the shirt, or saved that lamp from Instagram, telling an agent to buy it in my size at the best price is useful, the way a friend running an errand is useful. Telling it to find me a shirt and buy one is a different request, because the finding was the fun. Of the more than a dozen people I asked while working on this piece, hardly anyone was willing to hand an agent their shopping, and the few who were wanted to approve every purchase first.Every choice an agent makes for you is a prediction, and a prediction can only be built from what you have already done. That is fine for reordering coffee and far less useful for the choices that change a person, which tend to be the ones that break the pattern: the cuisine you have never tried, the film a friend dragged you to, the song playing in a shop that you spent the next morning tracking down.Ask anyone how they came to love a favourite writer, band or neighbourhood, and the answer is rarely a sensible shortlist. It is usually a detour.The agents' own early users have run into this. One, who wrote publicly about letting Meta's Muse run his life for two weeks, asked it how to spend money it had saved him, half expecting something generous. It suggested more of his favourite hobby. Nothing in his data said he might want to spend a windfall on someone else, so the option never appeared.That data is the price of entry. To find my boarding passes, Instinct had to read my inbox. To fill in my immigration form, it had to know my flights, my travel dates and where I had been staying. Every personal agent runs on the same bargain: to choose well for you, it has to read almost everything about you, and the record it builds is only as private as the company keeping it.The more you let an agent decide, the more that record describes only the person you have already been. Taste stops moving, because the things that used to move it, a stranger's recommendation, a bad decision that turned out well, a wrong turn, are exactly the inefficiencies the software was built to remove. Mark Zuckerberg has pitched Meta's agent as working "24/7 on your behalf to help achieve your goals and improve your life." That agent is wired into Facebook and Instagram, so whatever minutes it saves won't have far to travel.Most people don't spend spare time the way productivity software imagines. They spend it in small, aimless loops, sorting through old photos, reading the comments under a recipe they will never cook, taking the long way home, and the aimlessness is the point.Cooking is the clearest everyday case. A decade of meal kits and delivery apps has tried to automate it away, yet nearly half of Americans still named it as part of a good life when Gallup asked, against 6% for using AI tools.The agents, meanwhile, have plans for the quiet. Muse will happily ping you about a utility bill you have never once missed, and several others are designed to message first, before you have asked for anything. So the hours an agent saves you are quickly filled by the agent itself.None of this makes agents useless. The same Instinct that fumbled Berlin handled all the paperwork around that trip without fuss, and I was glad to let it. That is the kind of job an agent should be judged on: tedious, rule-bound and forgotten the moment it is done. It is also the bar every agent still on its way will have to clear. Nobody tells stories at dinner about forty minutes of hold music.That is the work worth handing over, and it is also where the access these agents demand starts to look reasonable. Only 13% of people in a Thales poll would let an AI helper read their email, and 7% would let one move money between accounts, a wall of reluctance no weekend plan will get past, though an end to customer service queues might.So who will we be when AI agents do the chores we secretly enjoy? Some of it depends on which side of that power-user profile you sit. The consultant living between airport lounges and back-to-back calls may well come out happier. Most of us sit on the other side of the ledger, shorter on cash than on hours, and those hours are where the fun lives: the long browse, the half-planned trip, the haggle over a secondhand chair.If we hand over only the dull chores, we stay much the same people, with fewer boarding passes to chase and the odd agent fetching a shirt we already picked out. If we hand over the choosing as well, we become people whose plans are drawn up from our own history, whose taste is a forecast and whose free time is free in the emptiest sense. Altman called booking a table trivial. It is also one of the small, daily ways people decide who they are, and that part is worth keeping out of an agent's hands.
Article Summary: AI agents are being built to take exactly these jobs away. They eat into our free time, and they are often the best part of it. People who pay for AI are five times as likely to use agents, according to Menlo Ventures and Morning Consult.
